title: Minimum Time Takes to Reach Destination Without Drowning
statement:
`land` is an `n` by `m` grid of one-character strings. You stand on the only `"S"` cell and want to reach the only `"D"` cell. Every other cell is `"."` (empty), `"X"` (stone) or `"*"` (already under water).

Time runs in whole seconds, and during each second two things happen together:

- You move to one of the up to four cells sharing a side with your current cell.
- The water spreads: every empty cell, and the start cell, that shares a side with a flooded cell becomes flooded. Water never enters stone or the `"D"` cell, so the destination stays dry.

You may never step onto stone, onto a flooded cell, or onto a cell that floods in the very second you arrive. Return the smallest number of seconds needed to reach `"D"`, or `-1` if it cannot be reached.
notes:
## Intuition

The water ignores you completely, so the second at which each cell floods can be worked out in advance with one multi-source BFS from every `"*"` cell. Once those times are known, your walk is an ordinary shortest-path BFS on the grid with one extra rule: you may enter a cell at second `t` only if it floods strictly later than `t`. Arriving early is never worse, because water only grows, so the first time BFS reaches a cell is the best time to be there. Simulating the water and every possible position second by second also works, but repeats the whole grid each second.

## Approach

1. Scan `land`: put every `"*"` cell in `water` with `floodTime` 0 and remember `start`.
2. BFS from `water`: a neighbour that is not stone, not `"D"` and not yet timed gets `floodTime` one more than its parent. Unreached cells keep `Infinity`.
3. BFS from `start` with `seconds` recording when you first stand on each cell.
4. Pop a cell; if it is `"D"`, return its `seconds`.
5. For each neighbour that is not stone and not visited, compute `arrival`; enter it only if `arrival < floodTime` there.
6. If the queue empties, return `-1`.

## Example 1, step by step

Water starts at (0,2). It reaches (0,1) and (1,2) at 1, (1,1) and (2,2) at 2, (1,0) and the start (2,1) at 3, and (2,0) at 4; `"D"` stays dry. From (2,1) you reach (1,1) at second 1 (floods at 2) and (2,0) at 1, then (1,0) at 2 (floods at 3), and finally `"D"` at (0,0) at second `3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n·m): each BFS handles every cell at most once.
- Space: O(n·m) for `floodTime`, `seconds` and the queues.

## Pitfalls

- Arriving in the same second the water arrives drowns you, so the test is `arrival >= floodTime`, not `>`.
- Water must not spread into `"D"` or `"X"`; letting it flood `"D"` would wrongly block a destination that stays dry.
- Cells the water never reaches need a time of `Infinity`, not 0 or -1, or the comparison blocks them.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `floodTime` | second at which each cell goes under water (`Infinity` if never) |
| `water` | BFS queue for the spreading water |
| `start` | position of `"S"` |
| `seconds` | second at which you first stand on each cell (-1 if not yet) |
| `queue`, `head` | BFS queue for your walk and its read position |
| `arrival` | second you would reach the neighbour being checked |
